chapter.name: How Forces Affect Motion
chapter.blurb: Building on the earlier description of motion, this chapter asks what causes it. It develops force as a quantity needing both magnitude and direction, distinguishes balanced from unbalanced forces, and studies the force of friction. It then states and applies Newton's three laws of motion -- inertia and the first law, F = ma and the second law, and the equal-and-opposite pairing of the third law -- through worked numerical examples, everyday applications such as airbags and rocket launches, and the idea of treating two connected objects as a single system.

scope_in.item: A force must be described by stating both its magnitude and its direction; forces named in earlier learning (friction, magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational, buoyant) are each described with a stated direction, and changing either the magnitude or the direction of a force changes its effect

The SI unit of force is the newton (symbol N); a spring balance measures the magnitude of a force in general, not only weight, and the weight of an object is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls it

Balanced forces (equal magnitude, opposite direction, zero net force) and unbalanced forces (non-zero net force); computing net force when two forces act along the same line, in the same or in opposite directions (tug-of-war example, Example 6.1)

The force of friction opposes the direction of motion and depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact (Activities 6.1 and 6.2); a spring-balance reading at the point an object just starts to move gives an approximate measure of the force of friction

Identifying all the forces acting on an object being pushed along a floor -- applied force, friction, weight (gravitational force) and normal force -- and that weight and normal force are balanced vertically; that air friction on a moving object is usually small enough to neglect

Newton's First Law of Motion: an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues with constant velocity, unless a net force acts on it; zero net force means zero acceleration; the meaning of 'at rest' (zero velocity) and 'constant velocity' (unchanging magnitude and direction)

The idea of inertia as the tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform motion, and Galileo's thought experiment (motion continuing indefinitely with no impediments) as the background to Newton's first law
Drawing and interpreting position-time and velocity-time graphs for an object with zero net force, for both the at-rest case and the constant-velocity case (Example 6.3)

Newton's Second Law of Motion: for a fixed mass, acceleration is proportional to the net force; for a fixed force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass; the equation a = F/m or F = ma, and one newton defined as the force that produces 1 m/s2 acceleration on a 1 kg mass
The gravitational force (weight) of an object, F = mg, with g approximately 9.8 m/s2 near the Earth's surface (or 10 m/s2 for quick estimates), and that g does not depend on the object's mass
Applying F = ma together with kinematic equations to find force, acceleration, mass or displacement, including from velocity-time graphs (Examples 6.4, 6.5, 6.6)

Real-world explanations using Newton's second law: why a cricket fielder's hands move back while catching a ball, why airbags reduce injury, and why a coconut's shell breaks on impact -- all through the idea that increasing or decreasing the time of a velocity change changes the force involved

Newton's Third Law of Motion: whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first; the two forces act on two different objects and so never balance each other; the law applies to contact forces and non-contact forces (magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational) alike

Everyday applications of Newton's third law: pushing off a table while seated on a wheeled chair, walking and running (the foot pushes the ground backward and friction from the ground pushes the person forward), climbing a tree trunk, paddling a canoe, and a balloon or rocket expelling gas to move in the opposite direction

Comparing the equal-magnitude forces of a Newton's third law pair with the very different accelerations they produce on objects of very different mass, using a = F/m (the Earth and a falling fruit, and a fired bullet and the recoiling gun, Examples 6.7 and 6.8)

Treating a system of two objects connected by a string, pulled by an external force on a frictionless surface, as a single combined object: the tension in the string is an internal force and can be left out, and the system's acceleration is a = F / (m1 + m2)
The external forces acting on a two-object connected system: the applied force, and the combined weight (m1+m2)g balanced by the combined normal force (N1+N2)

concepts.name: Force: magnitude, direction and measurement
concepts.description: Force as a quantity needing both magnitude and direction, its SI unit the newton, and how its magnitude is measured with a spring balance.
concepts.idea: A force must always be described together with its direction, not magnitude alone, and its magnitude can be measured with a spring balance.
concepts.rule: The SI unit of force is the newton (symbol N). Describing a force completely always needs both its magnitude and its direction; if either changes, the effect of the force also changes. A spring balance, commonly used to measure an object's weight (the gravitational force pulling it), can be used more generally to measure the magnitude of any pulling force.
concepts.example: A spring balance reading of 15 N when its hook is pulled tells you the magnitude of the pulling force is 15 N; to describe the force completely you would also need to state its direction, for example, '15 N to the east'.

questions.q: A magnet is brought near another magnet, and later a charged balloon is brought near another charged balloon. In both cases we are told 'like poles/charges repel, unlike attract'. questions.a: The phrasing 'like poles repel, unlike attract' (and similarly for charges) is telling us the direction of the magnetic or electrostatic force -- repel means the force pushes the two objects apart, attract means the force pulls them together -- alongside whatever magnitude the force has; this shows that describing any force, including magnetic and electrostatic forces, always requires stating its direction and not just its strength.
s: Identifies 'repel'/'attract' as specifying direction
Explains repel = apart, attract = together
Connects this to the general rule that a force needs magnitude and direction

questions.q: A friend says, 'I don't need to know the direction of a force if I already know its magnitude from a spring balance reading.' Do you agree? Justify your answer using an idea from the chapter.
questions.a: No, I do not agree; the chapter states that the effect of a force changes if either its magnitude or its direction changes, so knowing only the magnitude (from the spring balance reading) is not enough -- the direction must also be known to fully describe the force and predict its effect.
s: Clear position: disagree

questions.q: Design a short demonstration, different from the ones in the chapter, that could be used to show someone that a force needs a stated direction and not just a magnitude to be properly understood. Describe the demonstration and explain what it shows.
questions.a: For example, attach two identical spring balances to the same box, one pulling it to the north and one pulling it to the south, each reading exactly the same magnitude; even though the magnitudes are equal, whether the box stays still or moves (and in which direction) depends entirely on the directions of the two pulls, showing that magnitude alone cannot predict what happens -- the direction of each force must be known too.
s: Demonstration described, distinct from the book's own activities
Equal-magnitude forces used to isolate the role of direction
Explanation correctly ties the outcome to direction, not just magnitude

concepts.name: Balanced and unbalanced forces; net force
concepts.description: Combining two or more forces acting along the same line into a single net force, and distinguishing balanced forces (net force zero) from unbalanced forces (non-zero net force).
concepts.idea: When several forces act on an object along the same line, their combined effect is the net force: forces in the same direction add, forces in opposite directions subtract, and equal-and-opposite forces are balanced with zero net force.
concepts.rule: If forces act in the same direction, the net force magnitude is the sum of the magnitudes, in that same direction. If forces act in opposite directions, the net force magnitude is the difference of the magnitudes, in the direction of the larger force. If the opposing forces are exactly equal, the net force is zero and the forces are said to be balanced.
concepts.example: In a tug of war, if both teams pull with 10 N and 6 N respectively in opposite directions, the net force is 10 N - 6 N = 4 N towards the team pulling with 10 N, so the rope moves that way.

A is true, R is false

questions.a: Neither block experiences a net force: block P has two equal and opposite forces, which are balanced, so its net force is zero; block Q, moving with constant velocity, also has zero net force acting on it (its motion does not by itself indicate a net force).

questions.q: In a tug-of-war-like activity, five people pull a rope with a horizontal force of 200 N each in one direction, while a much larger group of 95 people pull with 200 N each in the opposite direction. Calculate the net force on the rope and explain in which direction the rope will move, and why this situation illustrates the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces.
questions.a: Force by the 5: 5 x 200 N = 1000 N. Force by the 95: 95 x 200 N = 19000 N. Net force = 19000 N - 1000 N = 18000 N, in the direction the group of 95 is pulling; the rope will move in that direction because the forces are unbalanced -- only when the two sides pull with exactly equal total force would the forces be balanced and the rope stay still.
s: Correctly computes both total forces (1000 N and 19000 N)
Correct net force 18000 N and correct direction
Explains the balanced vs unbalanced distinction correctly

concepts.name: Force of friction opposing motion
concepts.description: Friction as a force that opposes an object's motion and depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact, and how a spring balance can be used to approximately measure it.
concepts.idea: Friction is a force between two surfaces in contact that opposes relative motion between them, and its size depends on how rough or smooth the surfaces are.
concepts.rule: The force of friction acts opposite to the direction of motion (or the direction an object is being pushed). A rougher pair of surfaces gives more friction; a smoother pair gives less. The spring-balance reading needed to just start an object moving approximately measures the friction force between it and the surface.
concepts.example: A stack of coins given the same push travels much farther on polished marble than on a rough wooden table top, showing that friction is smaller on the marble surface.

The spring-balance readings when the block just starts moving are 6 N, 3 N, and 1 N respectively. Rank the three surfaces from largest to smallest force of friction, and predict on which surface the block, once set moving with the same push, will travel the farthest before stopping. Explain your reasoning.
questions.a: Ranking by friction, largest to smallest: sandpaper (6 N), wood (3 N), glass (1 N), since the spring-balance reading approximates the friction force. The block will travel farthest on the glass surface, because it has the smallest friction, so its velocity decreases most slowly and it takes the longest distance to come to rest.
s: Correct ranking of friction, largest to smallest
Correctly identifies glass as the surface with least friction
Correct explanation linking smaller friction to greater distance travelled

questions.q: Compare the forces acting on a box at the moment it is stationary (before being pushed) with the forces acting on it once it is moving at constant velocity after being pushed with a force equal to the friction force.
questions.a: When stationary, there is no net horizontal force, and the vertical weight and normal force are balanced. Once moving at constant velocity with the applied force equal to friction, the horizontal applied force and friction are balanced (equal and opposite), and the weight and normal force remain balanced vertically -- so in both cases the net force is zero, though in the second case two additional equal and opposite horizontal forces (applied force and friction) are present.
s: Correctly describes the stationary case (no net horizontal force, weight/normal balanced)

In the chapter's thought experiment, if an object were moving on a horizontal floor where the friction between them was exactly zero, the object's velocity would never decrease, and once set moving, it would continue moving forever at the same velocity, never coming to rest on its own.

concepts.name: Newton's First Law of Motion (law of inertia)
concepts.description: The statement of Newton's first law, the idea of inertia behind it, and drawing motion graphs for an object with zero net force.
concepts.idea: An object keeps doing whatever it was already doing -- staying at rest, or moving at constant velocity -- unless a net force acts on it to change that; this resistance to change is called inertia.
concepts.rule: Newton's First Law of Motion: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move with a constant velocity, unless a net force acts upon it. Equivalently, if the net force on an object is zero, its acceleration is zero.
concepts.example: A box pushed with a force exactly equal to the friction opposing it has zero net force, so by the first law it continues moving with constant velocity rather than speeding up or slowing down.

questions.q: A student says, 'if an object is moving, some force must be acting on it to keep it going.' Explain, using Newton's first law, why this statement is not correct in general.
questions.a: This statement is not correct in general; Newton's first law says that an object already moving with constant velocity continues to move with that same velocity if the net force on it is zero -- no force is needed to keep it going at a constant velocity. questions.q: Explain the connection between the idea of 'inertia' and Newton's First Law of Motion, and describe how Galileo's thought experiment about a body moving on a horizontal plane relates to this law.
questions.a: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform motion; Newton used this idea to frame his first law, which says an object continues in its state of rest or constant velocity unless a net force acts on it -- in other words, an object's inertia is what keeps it doing what it was already doing. Galileo had earlier argued, through a thought experiment, that if a body moves along a horizontal plane and all impediments (like friction) to its motion are removed, it would continue moving indefinitely; this idea -- that motion does not need a continuous force to sustain it -- became the basis for Newton's first law.
s: Correctly explains inertia as resistance to change in state of rest/motion
Correctly connects inertia to the statement of the first law
Correctly describes Galileo's thought experiment and its link to the law

questions.q: A classmate argues that Newton's first law is 'obviously wrong' because in everyday life, moving objects like a rolling ball or a cycling bicycle always eventually stop on their own, even without anyone applying a force to stop them. Evaluate this argument.
questions.a: The argument is flawed because it ignores that a net force -- the force of friction (and air resistance) -- is in fact acting on the ball or bicycle in everyday situations, opposing its motion; Newton's first law only predicts that an object keeps moving at constant velocity when there is truly no net force acting on it, which is rarely the case in everyday life because friction is almost always present.
s: Identifies the flaw: friction is a net force that is present, not absent
Correctly reconciles everyday slowing-down with the first law's actual condition (zero net force)

questions.q: Describe a situation from daily life, different from any example in the chapter, where you could point to Newton's first law being demonstrated, and explain clearly which part of the object's motion (staying at rest, or continuing at constant velocity) illustrates the law, and what net force condition applies.
questions.a: For example, a coin placed on a smooth table remains exactly where it is placed until someone flicks it -- this shows the 'object at rest remains at rest' part of the law, because as long as no net force acts on the coin (the tiny friction with the table and its own weight are balanced by the table's normal force), it does not move on its own. Once flicked, if the table were frictionless, the coin would keep sliding at constant velocity forever, illustrating the 'constant velocity continues' part of the law under zero net force.
s: A valid, original daily-life example is described
Correctly identifies which part of the law (rest or constant motion) it illustrates
Correctly explains the net-force condition (zero net force) involved

concepts.name: Newton's Second Law of Motion: F = ma
concepts.description: The relationship between net force, mass and acceleration, the definition of the newton, the weight formula F = mg, and applying F = ma with kinematics.
concepts.idea: A net force produces an acceleration in its own direction; for the same object a bigger force gives a bigger acceleration, and for the same force a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration.
concepts.rule: Newton's Second Law: acceleration a = F/m, or F = ma, where F is the net force, m the mass and a the acceleration, all in the same direction. One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s2. The weight of an object is F = mg, where g is about 9.8 m/s2 near the Earth's surface and does not depend on the object's mass.
concepts.example: A weightlifter holding a 30 kg barbell steady must apply an upward force equal to its weight: F = mg = 30 kg x 9.8 m/s2 = 294 N.

concepts.name: Newton's Third Law of Motion: action and reaction
concepts.description: The statement of Newton's third law, why the two forces in a pair act on different objects and never balance each other, and everyday and numerical applications.
concepts.idea: Forces always occur in equal-and-opposite pairs, one on each of two different interacting objects, so the two forces of a pair never balance each other even though they are equal in magnitude.
concepts.rule: Newton's Third Law: Whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force on the first object. This applies to both contact forces (like pushing) and non-contact forces (like gravity, magnetism and electrostatic attraction/repulsion). Because the two forces of a pair act on different objects with (usually) different masses, they generally produce very different accelerations (a = F/m).
concepts.example: When a canoeist pushes water backward with a paddle, the water pushes the paddle (and canoe) forward with an equal and opposite force, moving the canoe forward.

By Newton's third law, the apple also pulls the Earth with an equal and opposite force of 1 N. Given the Earth's mass is about 6 x 10^24 kg, calculate the apple's acceleration and estimate the order of magnitude of the Earth's acceleration due to this force, and use this to explain why we see the apple fall but never see the Earth move.
questions.a: Apple's acceleration = F/m = 1 N / 0.1 kg = 10 m/s2 (close to g). Earth's acceleration = F/m = 1 N / (6 x 10^24 kg), which is about 1.7 x 10^-25 m/s2, an extremely tiny value. Because the Earth's mass is so enormous compared to the apple's, the force -- though equal in magnitude to the force on the apple -- produces an immeasurably small acceleration on the Earth, so its motion is far too small to ever notice, while the apple, with its tiny mass, visibly accelerates and falls.

questions.q: A classmate says, 'since the ground pushes back on my feet with an equal and opposite force whenever I push it, I should never be able to walk forward at all -- the forces should cancel out.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: This claim is incorrect; the two forces (the foot pushing the ground backward, and the ground pushing the foot forward) are equal and opposite but act on two different objects -- the ground and the foot/person -- so by Newton's third law they do not cancel each other out. Only forces acting on the same object can balance each other; here, the forward force from the ground on the person is what actually causes the person to accelerate forward and walk.
s: Correctly identifies the flaw: the forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel
Correctly explains that it is the ground's forward force on the person that causes walking

questions.q: Think of an everyday activity, different from walking, climbing, canoeing, or rocket launching, that depends on Newton's third law to work. Describe the activity, identify the action force and the reaction force, and explain which object's motion we actually notice as a result.
questions.a: For example, when a swimmer pushes water backward with their arms and legs during a swimming stroke, the action force is the swimmer pushing the water backward, and by Newton's third law, the reaction force is the water pushing the swimmer forward with an equal and opposite force; we notice the swimmer's own forward motion through the water as a result of this reaction force, since the swimmer's mass is what is free to accelerate forward, unlike the huge mass of water around them.
s: A valid, original everyday example is described
Action and reaction forces correctly identified
Correctly explains which object's motion is noticeably observed and why

concepts.name: Forces on a system of connected objects
concepts.description: Treating two objects connected by a string as a single combined system to find their common acceleration, without needing to find the internal tension force.
concepts.idea: Two connected objects pulled by an external force move with the same acceleration and can be treated as one combined object; the tension in the string connecting them is an internal force that can be left out of this whole-system calculation.
concepts.rule: For two objects of mass m1 and m2 connected by a string and pulled by an external force F (on a frictionless surface), the acceleration of the system is a = F / (m1 + m2); the tension in the string is an internal force (an equal-and-opposite Newton's-third-law pair between the two objects) and does not need to be found to get this acceleration.
concepts.example: Two boxes of mass 2 kg and 3 kg connected by a string and pulled by a force of 10 N have a combined acceleration of a = 10 N / (2 kg + 3 kg) = 2 m/s2.

questions.q: When analysing a system of two objects connected together, the tension force in the connecting string is treated as
questions.a: an internal force of the system
o: an internal force of the system
an external force of the system
irrelevant and always ignored
the only force acting on the system

questions.q: For a system of two connected boxes of masses m1 and m2 pulled by an external force F, the acceleration of the system is a = F / ____.
questions.a: m1 + m2

questions.q: In a system of two boxes connected by a string, which force do you NOT need to calculate separately if you treat the two boxes and the string as a single system?
questions.a: the tension force in the string
o: the tension force in the string
the external applied force
the total mass of the system
the resulting acceleration of the system

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true about treating two connected boxes as a single system?
questions.a: the tension acting on each box must still be calculated separately even to find the system's acceleration
o: the tension acting on each box must still be calculated separately even to find the system's acceleration
the system accelerates like a single object of mass (m1+m2)
only external forces need to be considered for the system's acceleration
internal forces like tension do not need to be found to get the system's acceleration

questions.q: In the two-box system pulled by a force F, which force acts on Box 1 alone but not directly on Box 2?
questions.a: the applied external force F
o: the applied external force F
the tension force T
the gravitational force on the whole system
the normal force on the whole system

questions.q: The force that Box 1 exerts on Box 2 through the connecting string, and the equal and opposite force Box 2 exerts back on Box 1, is called ____.
questions.a: tension

questions.q: Treating a two-box system as a single object of combined mass usually makes the analysis
questions.a: simpler, since only external forces need to be considered
o: simpler, since only external forces need to be considered
more complicated, since more forces must be tracked
impossible, since Newton's laws do not apply to systems
only valid if the boxes have equal mass

questions.q: For the two-box system on a frictionless surface, the vertical forces on the system are
questions.a: the combined weight (m1+m2)g downward, balanced by the combined normal force (N1+N2) upward
o: the combined weight (m1+m2)g downward, balanced by the combined normal force (N1+N2) upward
only the combined weight, with no balancing force
the tension force T acting vertically
only the normal force, with no weight acting

questions.q: Explain why the tension in the string connecting two boxes does not need to be included when finding the acceleration of the whole two-box system.
questions.a: The tension is an internal force of the system -- by Newton's third law, Box 1 pulls Box 2 with tension T and Box 2 pulls Box 1 back with an equal and opposite tension T, so these two internal forces act within the system and effectively cancel out when considering the system as a whole; only external forces, like the applied force F, determine the system's overall acceleration.
s: Identifies tension as an internal, third-law pair of forces within the system
Explains that internal forces cancel out for the system, so only external forces matter

questions.q: Two boxes of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are connected by a string and pulled by a force of 10 N on a frictionless surface. The acceleration of the system is
questions.a: 2 m/s2
o: 2 m/s2
5 m/s2
1 m/s2

questions.q: A system made of two connected trolleys of total mass 20 kg is pulled by an external force of 40 N with no friction. The acceleration of the system is
questions.a: 2 m/s2
o: 2 m/s2

questions.q: Two crates of mass 4 kg and 6 kg are connected by a string on a frictionless floor and pulled by a horizontal force of 30 N. Calculate the acceleration of the system.
questions.a: Total mass = 4 kg + 6 kg = 10 kg. Acceleration = F / (m1+m2) = 30 N / 10 kg = 3 m/s2.
s: Correct total mass (10 kg)
Correct acceleration (3 m/s2)

questions.q: A train engine of mass 8000 kg pulls a single bogie of mass 2000 kg with a force of 20000 N, with no friction. Treating the engine and bogie as one system, find the system's acceleration.
questions.a: Total mass = 8000 kg + 2000 kg = 10000 kg. Acceleration = F / total mass = 20000 N / 10000 kg = 2 m/s2.
s: Correct total mass (10000 kg)
Correct acceleration (2 m/s2)

questions.q: Two boxes of masses 5 kg and 10 kg are connected by a string and pulled together by a force of 45 N on a frictionless surface. The acceleration of the system is
questions.a: 3 m/s2
o: 3 m/s2
9 m/s2

questions.q: A tractor pulling only a harrow of mass 300 kg with a force F produces an acceleration of 2 m/s2. The same tractor pulling only a trolley of mass 600 kg with the same force F produces some acceleration. First find F, then find the trolley's acceleration when pulled alone, and finally find the acceleration when the tractor pulls the trolley with the harrow loaded onto it, using the same force F.
questions.a: F = m1 x a1 = 300 kg x 2 m/s2 = 600 N. Trolley alone: a2 = F/m2 = 600 N / 600 kg = 1 m/s2. Harrow loaded onto trolley (combined system, mass 300+600=900 kg): a = F/(m1+m2) = 600 N / 900 kg = about 0.67 m/s2.
s: Correctly finds F = 600 N
Correctly finds the trolley's own acceleration (1 m/s2)
Correctly finds the combined system's acceleration (about 0.67 m/s2)

questions.q: Consider a system of two boxes connected by a string and pulled by an external force: (I) The tension in the string is an external force on the system. (II) The system's acceleration can be found using only the total mass and the external force. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II
o: Only II
Only I
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

questions.q: Two systems are pulled by the same external force F: System A has a total mass of 5 kg, and System B has a total mass of 20 kg. Compare their accelerations, and explain your reasoning using the system formula a = F / total mass.
questions.a: System A has the greater acceleration, since for the same force F, a smaller total mass gives a larger acceleration (a = F / total mass); System B, having four times the mass of System A, would have only a quarter of System A's acceleration for the same force.
s: Correctly identifies System A as having the greater acceleration
Correct reasoning using a = F / total mass, including the quarter/four-times relationship

questions.q: Two boxes of masses m1 and m2 are connected by a string and pulled by a force F on a frictionless floor. Explain, using Newton's laws, both why the two boxes must have the same acceleration as each other, and why the whole system's acceleration can be correctly found using a = F/(m1+m2) without separately calculating the tension in the string.
questions.a: The two boxes are connected by an inextensible string, so they must always move together with the same acceleration -- they cannot speed up or slow down independently while remaining connected. The tension in the string is an internal force: by Newton's third law, Box 1 exerts a force T on Box 2 through the string, and Box 2 exerts an equal and opposite force T back on Box 1; when the two boxes and the string are considered together as a single system, these two internal tension forces act on parts of the same system in opposite directions and do not affect the system's overall motion, so only the external force F and the total mass (m1+m2) are needed to find the system's acceleration, using Newton's second law applied to the system as a whole.
s: Correctly explains why both boxes share the same acceleration (connected, inextensible string)
Correctly identifies tension as an internal, third-law pair force
Correctly explains why internal forces can be ignored when applying Newton's second law to the whole system

questions.q: A classmate says, 'treating two connected boxes as one system must give a wrong answer, because we are ignoring the tension force in the string.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: This claim is incorrect; tension is an internal force of the system, and internal forces occur in equal-and-opposite (Newton's third law) pairs that do not change the system's overall motion, so they can be left out when finding the system's acceleration using only external forces and the total mass -- this gives the correct acceleration, not a wrong one; tension would only need to be calculated separately if we wanted to know the force acting on just one of the two boxes individually.
s: Correctly rejects the claim as incorrect, with valid reasoning
Correctly explains when tension would actually need to be calculated (analysing one box alone)

questions.q: Design your own example of two objects connected together and pulled by an external force (choose your own masses and force, different from any used elsewhere in this concept), and calculate the acceleration of the system, showing your working clearly.
questions.a: For example, two connected sleds of mass 7 kg and 13 kg are pulled by a force of 60 N on frictionless snow. Total mass = 7 kg + 13 kg = 20 kg. Acceleration = F / total mass = 60 N / 20 kg = 3 m/s2.
s: An original example with chosen masses and force is designed
Correct total mass calculated
Correct final acceleration calculated and shown clearly
